summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force on the islands is Dutch national law, applied there in the same form as in the European Netherlands, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes any provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

Travel coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 places Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, citing its standing as part of the Netherlands, under whose strict anti-discrimination laws it says citizens and visitors are protected, and describing same-sex couples as warmly welcomed.

Registered unions for same-sex couples have been available in the islands since 2012. The first was recorded by the Census Office in Saba on 4 December 2012: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on Saba and both were visiting, which establishes that the island registry performs ceremonies for couples who are only passing through.

Saba Tourism's weddings page states that civil ceremonies run routinely through the island registry, that the Court Room in the Administrative Building is the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony, and that registrar Julieta Woods is flexible with couples' wishes. Caterers, florists and accommodation serving destination weddings operate on the island.
tangentialFactors:
The fifth-place entry in the GayCities list is a comparative claim, but the list is a travel publication's assessment of hospitality covering ten destinations, not a legal index. What it reflects is the reach of Dutch national anti-discrimination law into the islands rather than any island-level statute of its own.

The 2012 registration involved two visitors rather than residents, so the documented practice concerns couples travelling to the islands to marry. That makes the record of performing ceremonies for people who are passing through direct, rather than inferred from resident marriages.
localsOnly:
Civil-status registration is handled at island level; the Census Office in Saba recorded the territory's first registered same-sex union in 2012. Residents in same-sex relationships have had access to registered unions since that year.

The 2012 record concerns two non-resident men, so no source in the inventory shows the uptake of registration among island residents, the documentation an island registrar requires from a resident couple, or how a resident couple's identity papers are handled. The registrar's documented flexibility is described for ceremonies generally, without distinguishing residents from visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry or immigration screening, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors. The findings above rest on marriage registration and anti-discrimination provisions rather than on trans-specific legal text.

Anti-discrimination coverage is asserted in travel-facing coverage rather than documented through a statutory citation, an equality body's decisions or complaint data; no enforcement record for the islands appears in the inventory.

Sint Eustatius is not addressed separately in any source, and the documented ceremonial practice is drawn from Saba. No source reports violence, police conduct or complaints data for any of the three islands.
